title: Chemical Bonding & Structure Adventure 3: Giant structures and hybridisation
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet giant covalent diamond and graphite — and hybridise carbon.
meta_desc: IBDP Chemistry — giant covalent, diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes, sp/sp²/sp³ hybridisation.
final_note: You learned giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, SiO₂) have very high mp, allotropes of carbon include graphene and fullerenes, and hybridisation explains bond geometry.

concepts.def: Each C sp³ to 4 others; hardest

walkthroughs.body_html:
Both are pure carbon — but very different.

Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others tetrahedrally; sp³. Hardest natural substance, electrical insulator (no free e⁻).

Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal sheets; sp². Layers slide (lubricant), delocalised e⁻ above/below conduct electricity.

Graphene (Geim + Novoselov, Nobel 2010): single sheet of graphite. Strongest material known, transparent, conducts.

Fullerenes like C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene, 1985): football-shaped molecules. Used in drug delivery, electronics.

Carbon nanotubes: rolled graphene; super strong, conducting.

Mixing s + p orbitals gives equivalent hybrid orbitals:

- sp³ (1s + 3p = 4) — tetrahedral, 109.5°. CH₄, diamond.
- sp² (1s + 2p = 3) — trigonal planar, 120°. C=C in ethene, graphite. Remaining p forms π bond.
- sp (1s + 1p = 2) — linear, 180°. C≡C in ethyne. Two π bonds.
